name: Otúke
confidence_why: Otúke has been extinct since the nineteenth century and survives only in d'Orbigny's 1831 vocabulary of about 300 words as published by Créqui-Montfort & Rivet (1912), whose transcription marks no stressed syllables; Camargos (2013: 101) accordingly states that the syllable bearing stress cannot be identified, and d'Orbigny (1839) and Créqui-Montfort & Rivet (1912, 1913) say nothing about accent.
catalog_citation: Camargos, Lidiane Szerwinsk. 2013. Consolidando uma proposta de família linguística Boróro: contribuição aos estudos histórico-comparativos do tronco Macro-Jê. PhD dissertation, Universidade de Brasília. 253 pp.
catalog_locator: sec. 4.9 'Acento', p. 101; also sec. 4.7.3 'Língua Otúke', p. 99
catalog_quote: 4.9. Acento De acordo com Rodrigues (2007), na língua Boróro o acento de intensidade recai sistematicamente sobre a penúltima sílaba de cada palavra. Sobre a língua Umutína, o autor (op. cit.) assinala que embora não haja um consenso entre Shultz (1952), Schmidt (1941) e Lima (1995) na marcação do acento, este ocorre predominantemente na última sílaba das palavras. Com relação ao acento da língua Otúke, verifica-se que a ausência absoluta de dados sonoros e a omissão na marcação de sílabas fortes pelo viajante Alcides d’Orbigny (1831) durante a coleta de dados, não permite a identificação sobre a sílaba em que recai o acento de intensidade nessa língua.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.translation: According to Rodrigues (2007), in the Bororo language intensity stress falls systematically on the penultimate syllable of each word. For the Umutina language the same author notes that, although there is no consensus among Schultz (1952), Schmidt (1941) and Lima (1995) in the marking of stress, it occurs predominantly on the last syllable of words. As for stress in the Otuke language, the complete absence of sound data and the omission of any marking of strong syllables by the traveller Alcide d'Orbigny (1831) during data collection do not allow identification of the syllable on which intensity stress falls in this language.
new_statements.citation: Camargos, Lidiane Szerwinsk. 2013. Consolidando uma proposta de família linguística Boróro: contribuição aos estudos histórico-comparativos do tronco Macro-Jê. PhD dissertation, Universidade de Brasília.
new_statements.locator: sec. 4.9 'Acento', p. 101 (PDF page 122); see also sec. 4.7.3 'Língua Otúke', p. 99 (PDF page 120)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Camargos 2013, (extracted text of the 253-page PDF), form-feed page 122 = printed p. 101, heading '4.9. Acento' (the text): both sentences of the quote are present word for word, including 'Shultz (1952)' and 'Alcides d'Orbigny (1831)'; the compiler merely joined two paragraphs ('..última sílaba das palavras.' / 'Com relação ao acento da língua Otúke..') into one quote. The second sentence on p. 99 (p. 120, sec. 4.7.3 'Língua Otúke', lines 4832-4834) is also verbatim: 'não há nenhum registro de dados sonoros da língua Otúke ou marcação de acento nos dados coletados originalmente por D'Orbigny (1831)'. I read secs. 4.7.3-4.10 (pp. 120-122): p. 100 gives the Otuke syllable patterns V, CV, CVC…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for Otuke and the earlier scan found no source; Camargos 2013 is the first opened source that addresses Otuke stress at all, and it states explicitly why no placement can be recovered (no audio, no accent marks in the sole wordlist). Compatible with the empty catalog entry and with the silence of Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1912/1913 and d'Orbigny 1839 already recorded; adds the sister-language context (Bororo penultimate, Umutina predominantly final).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule can be stated: the only source of Otuke data (d'Orbigny's 1831 vocabulary, published by Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1912/1913) marks no stressed syllables and no sound recordings exist, so the position of word stress in Otuke is explicitly declared unidentifiable. Sec. 4.7.3, p. 99 says the same in passing: 'não há nenhum registro de dados sonoros da língua Otúke ou marcação de acento nos dados coletados originalmente por D'Orbigny (1831)'. For family context the same paragraph gives Bororo = fixed penultimate (citing Rodrigues 2007) and Umutina = predominantly final. Otuke syllable patterns V, CV, CVC, CCV, with CV most productive (pp. 99-100).
new_statements.identity_note: Camargos 2013 treats 'Otúke' as d'Orbigny's 1831 vocabulary (299 words, via Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1912, 1913) and keeps Kovareka and Kuruminaka apart as separate closely related languages known only from 14- and 19-word lists; the stress statement quoted is about Otuke proper. Bororo and Umutina placements in the same paragraph are about those sister languages, not Otuke.

sources.citation: Créqui-Montfort, Georges de & Paul Rivet. 1912. Linguistique bolivienne. Le groupe Otuké. Journal de la Société des Américanistes de Paris n.s. 9: 317-337.
sources.note: The only primary data: d'Orbigny's 1831 vocabulary (299 words) with 19- and 14-word Kovareka/Kuruminaka lists. Transcription note p. 318 fn. 2 defines a uniform notation (é = French é, etc.) and diacritics for 'nasal et guttural' vowels; the acute marks vowel quality only. pp. 321-326 give sound correspondences (c ~ y), prefix i-, suffixes -ra, -ka, -vi, -to, -ri, -ru, -huari, compounds, pronouns, verb endings -ta/-take. No word on accent, stress, tone or syllable prominence anywhere in the article.

sources.citation: Mulder, Sophie. 2024. Otuke: reviewing the only remaining data on an extinct Bolivian language. MA thesis, Leiden University (supervisor E.I. Crevels).
sources.note: The only modern study of the Otuke data; abstract promises 'an overview of phonological and morphological processes present in Otuke'. Could conceivably comment on accent marks in d'Orbigny's manuscript, though the abstract does not mention prosody; open access per the repository page but blocked by a bot-check to non-browser clients.

sources.citation: Créqui-Montfort, Georges de & Paul Rivet. 1913. Linguistique bolivienne. Les affinités des dialectes Otuké. Journal de la Société des Américanistes de Paris n.s. 10: 369-377.
sources.note: Lexical comparison Otuke ~ Bororo (Steinen, Colbacchini, Frič data) and consonant correspondences (Otuke c/s ~ Bororo k; Bororo g,k ~ Otuke h; ba ~ vua/hua; t ~ h; u ~ vu), possessive prefixes i-, te-. Nothing on accent or stress.

sources.citation: d'Orbigny, Alcide. 1839. Voyage dans l'Amérique méridionale, t. IV, 1re partie: L'homme américain (de l'Amérique méridionale) considéré sous ses rapports physiologiques et moraux. Paris: Pitois-Levrault. 'Nation Otukès', pp. 268-269.
sources.note: pp. 268-269: 'La langue otukè n'a aucune gutturation, très-peu de diphthongues ou de sons venant du nez. Elle est des plus douce et des plus facile soit à entendre, soit à écrire.. la langue manque absolument de z et d's simple. Ses mots ne finissent jamais par une consonne, mais toujours par les voyelles'; body-part nouns begin with i-. Nothing on accent for Otuke; only a general remark elsewhere that 'Toutes les langues américaines sont fortement accentuées' (not language-specific).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page otuk1240 and Wikipedia 'Otuke language' (reference lists only).
sources.note: Glottolog lists no descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) reference, only Camargos 2013 for subclassification; Wikipedia's reference list adds Loukotka 1949, Combès 2012, Mason 1950, Campbell 2024 (none descriptive). No stress information.
